summary: Describes the binding protocols used with ONC RPC version 2, which help clients find the right service on a server. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: An ONC RPC client needs a network address before it can call a service, but the service's port may change. This RFC defines a lookup service that lets servers publish their addresses and clients find them.

questions: how does onc rpc binding work
what is a universal address in onc rpc
subtitle: How ONC RPC clients find the network address of a service whose port can change.

tldr.problem: An ONC RPC client knows the service program and version, but the server's transport port may be chosen dynamically.
tldr.mechanism: A server registers its address with a lookup service. Clients query that service; newer RPCBIND versions represent addresses as transport-independent text.
tldr.outcome: The document defines RPCBIND versions 3 and 4 and the older Port Mapper version 2. RFC 5665 later updates it.

today: RFC 1833 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5665; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why RPC Uses a Lookup Service
sections.content:
An ONC Remote Procedure Call (RPC) service is identified by a program number, a version number and a transport address. For TCP/IP or UDP/IP, that address includes an IP address and a port. The port is often assigned dynamically, so the client cannot rely on a fixed value.

The server registers its address with a lookup service at a known address. The client asks that service for the address associated with the program and version it needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The client knows which service it wants, but may not know its current network address. The server records that address in a lookup service so the client can ask for it.

sections.title: RPCBIND Uses Universal Addresses
sections.content:
RPCBIND versions 3 and 4 map program and version numbers to universal addresses. A universal address is an ASCII text form of an address for a particular transport. The transport's addressing rules define how that text is written, so RPCBIND can support transports beyond TCP and UDP.

A registration includes the program, version, local network identifier, universal address and service owner. The network identifier follows local conventions and may differ between machines. RPCBIND can also relay broadcast calls to the local service on each machine that receives the broadcast.
sections.plainLanguage: RPCBIND stores an address as text whose format is defined for its transport. That lets the same lookup protocol describe addresses for different kinds of networks.

sections.title: Registering and Looking Up a Service
sections.content:
A service uses SET when it becomes available and UNSET when it stops. SET refuses a duplicate mapping for the same program, version and network identifier. Only the service owner or super-user may remove a mapping with UNSET.

GETADDR returns the address for a service, while DUMP lists the database. Other procedures convert between universal and transport-specific addresses, return server time or statistics, and make an indirect call. Version 4 adds exact-version lookup, address lists and separate names for broadcast and indirect calls.

Clients on other machines can call every procedure except SET and UNSET. RPCBIND accepts those changes only from a client on the same machine.
sections.plainLanguage: A service adds its address when it starts and removes it when it stops. Clients can ask where it is, but only a local client can change the registrations.

sections.title: The Port Mapper, Version 2
sections.content:
The Port Mapper is the older, transport-specific lookup protocol. It maps an RPC program and version plus a protocol number to a TCP or UDP port. Clients contact it on port 111, using either TCP or UDP.

GETPORT returns the registered port; zero means that the service has no registration. DUMP lists all mappings. CALLIT can invoke a remote procedure without the client knowing its port, but the Port Mapper contacts that procedure using UDP and replies only when the call succeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: The older Port Mapper understands TCP and UDP port numbers directly. If it returns zero, the service has not registered a port.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It does specify a local-access rule for RPCBIND: only clients on the same machine may register or remove services.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not analyze security. It limits registration changes to clients running on the same machine as RPCBIND.
